raw_case_text:
The patient was a 60 year old European homosexual man who had HIV infection diagnosed in 1985. Zidovudine monotherapy was commenced in 1988 and three-drug combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) in 1996. His ART between 2001 and 2013 consisted of lopinavir/ritonavir, lamivudine and nevirapine. He had a prompt sustained response to ART and from 1997-2013 consistently had an undetectable HIV viral load. Despite this, his CD4 count, which had a nadir of 39 in 1996, never rose above 140 despite consistent adherence to his ART (Fig 1A).
In April 1996 he developed drenching sweats and hepato-splenomegaly, and in March 1997 the diagnosis of VL was confirmed by the visualization of amastigotes in bone marrow samples. Infection with Leishmania infantum had probably been acquired during a visit to Spain in 1992. Initial treatment with sodium stibogluconate 20 mg/kg for 44 days over 8 weeks achieved a clinical improvement and clearance of parasites from his bone marrow.
Visceral leishmaniasis relapsed in July 1997 and persisted for the next 15 years, despite combination treatment with: paromomycin 15 mg/kg and stibogluconate; stibogluconate, liposomal amphotericin 3mg/kg and gamma interferon 2 megaunits subcutaneously; and since 2000 with 7 days liposomal amphotericin 3 mg/kg daily every 6 weeks, increasing to every 3 weeks in May 2012. Miltefosine 50 mg twice daily, for 28 days every 3 months, was added in March 2005.
 Leishmania amastigotes were visualized in bone marrow samples collected in September 2004, March, May, and December 2005, November 2006, October 2007, and February 2011; and also in skin lesions biopsied in November 2003, September 2007, and May 2009; lymph nodes biopsied in May 2009 and September 2011; and a sigmoid biopsy in March 2000. An isolate of Leishmania infantum cultured from a bone marrow aspirate in October 2007 was tested at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine in January 2008 and reported to be resistant to stibogluconate (IC50 > 60 mg/L) but susceptible to amphotericin B (IC50 = 0.3 muM), miltefosine (IC50 = 8 muM) and paromomycin (IC50 = 4 muM).
Treatment of VL was complicated by significant adverse drug effects including: marked visual impairment presumed secondary to antimonial toxicity; hearing loss presumed secondary to various agents including paromomycin; and multiple episodes of bacteremia arising from the indwelling cannula used for his IV infusions of liposomal amphotericin B. The patient suffered increasing discomfort from his splenomegaly and had an increasing requirement for red cell transfusions. In view of his worsening symptoms and pancytopenia, and the consistent increase in the density of amastigotes in his bone marrow samples despite maximal conventional treatment, alternative therapeutic approaches were discussed at length with the patient and with experts elsewhere.
With written informed consent from the patient, and agreement from the Hospital Medicines Committee, he received six doses of intravenous liposomal daunorubicin: 34mg on 24 October 2012, 50mg on 7 November, 50 mg on 21 November, 40mg on 7 January 2013, 50mg on 21 January, and 50mg on 4 February. Daunorubicin was chosen instead of doxorubicin because of personal and institutional experience in the use of this agent for the treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma in patients with HIV infection. The treatment regimen was based on that recommended for the treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma in patients with HIV infection and mild renal impairment. The patient was carefully monitored for evidence of cardiotoxicity, and other potential adverse effects of daunorubicin therapy. Each treatment resulted in a temporary worsening of his pancytopenia but there were no significant infectious, bleeding or other adverse effects (Fig 1B). There was no decrease in his splenomegaly either on clinical examination or on abdominal imaging (Fig 2). The density of amastigotes in the bone marrow trephine collected 7 days after the last dose of daunorubicin was greater than that in the most recent previous trephine which had been collected in February 2011 (Fig 3). Urine samples collected on May 8 2013, 3 months after the last dose of daunorubicin, showed 3+ agglutination using the KAtex Leishmania urinary antigen detection test. In September 2013, 7 months after the completion of the trial of daunorubicin, the patient was in an unchanged clinical condition compared to the immediate pre-treatment period, with persistent abdominal pain due to severe hepato-splenomegaly, pancytopenia and disabling lethargy. The patient decided to cease all treatment of his HIV infection, VL, and other medical conditions. He died of complications of VL within one month of stopping treatment.
The patient provided written informed consent for all procedures (skin biopsy, bone marrow biopsy, and sigmoidoscopy and biopsy) and written informed consent for the trial of liposomal daunorubicin. The Hospital Medicines Committee approved the trial of liposomal daunorubicin.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male with HIV infection presented with drenching sweats, massive splenomegaly, and pancytopenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 60-year-old HIV-infected male presented in April 1996 with drenching night sweats and hepatosplenomegaly. Parasitic visceral infection was diagnosed in March 1997. Despite initial antimonial response, the illness relapsed in July 1997 and persisted for 15 years as refractory disease despite multidrug antileishmanial regimens. He developed progressive splenomegaly causing severe abdominal pain, worsening pancytopenia requiring frequent red cell transfusions, and adverse drug toxicities. In October 2012 to February 2013, he consented to an experimental trial of intravenous liposomal daunorubicin. In September 2013, facing persistent severe hepato-splenomegaly, transfusion-dependent pancytopenia, and disabling lethargy, he elected to withdraw all therapy and entered palliative care.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 1985; treated with zidovudine monotherapy (1988), combination ART (1996), and lopinavir/ritonavir, lamivudine, nevirapine (2001-2013). Travel history: travel to Spain in 1992. Chronic medical complications: mild renal impairment, marked visual impairment attributed to antimonial toxicity, hearing loss secondary to paromomycin, and recurrent central line-associated bacteremias.
subjective.review_of_systems: Drenching sweats, severe abdominal discomfort and fullness from splenomegaly, profound fatigue and disabling lethargy, visual impairment, hearing loss. Denied fever during late stages.

objective.physical_examination: Severe, massive hepatosplenomegaly causing abdominal distension and palpable splenic enlargement filling the left abdomen. Indwelling central venous catheter in situ. Conjunctival pallor.
objective.routine_investigations: Progressive pancytopenia requiring repeated packed red blood cell transfusions. HIV-1 RNA viral load consistently undetectable (< 50 copies/mL) from 1997 to 2013. CD4+ T-cell count had a nadir of 39 cells/muL in 1996 and remained persistently < 140 cells/muL despite adherence to ART. Mild renal impairment. Urine KAtex urinary antigen test: 3+ agglutination (May 2013).
objective.advanced_workup: Serial bone marrow trephine biopsies (1997, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2011, and post-daunorubicin 2013) demonstrated heavy and increasing infiltration of macrophages with intracellular microorganisms. Histopathology of skin biopsies (2003, 2007, 2009), lymph node biopsies (2009, 2011), and sigmoid colon biopsy (2000) revealed disseminated intracellular organisms. Abdominal imaging (CT) confirmed persistent massive splenomegaly without regression. Serial electrocardiograms and cardiac monitoring revealed no daunorubicin cardiotoxicity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Refractory, multidrug-resistant visceral leishmaniasis with multiorgan dissemination (skin, lymph nodes, and sigmoid colon) in a patient with HIV-1 infection and severe immunological non-response.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct visualization of Leishmania amastigotes in serial bone marrow aspirates/trephines, skin lesions, lymph nodes, and sigmoid mucosa. Culture from bone marrow (October 2007) yielded Leishmania infantum; in vitro susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to sodium stibogluconate (IC50 > 60 mg/L), but susceptibility to amphotericin B (IC50 = 0.3 muM), miltefosine (IC50 = 8 muM), and paromomycin (IC50 = 4 muM). Positive urine KAtex antigen detection test (3+ agglutination).
Differentials Ruled Out: Kaposi's sarcoma (biopsies negative for spindle cell proliferation / HHV8), lymphoma, mycobacteriosis, and opportunistic fungal infections.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Multiple combination antileishmanial regimens over 15 years: sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg), paromomycin (15 mg/kg), liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg daily, transitioned to maintenance every 6 then 3 weeks), subcutaneous interferon-gamma (2 MU), and oral miltefosine (50 mg BID). In October 2012-February 2013, administered 6 cycles of liposomal daunorubicin (34-50 mg IV per dose) with transient bone marrow suppression but no reduction in parasite density or spleen size. In September 2013, the patient ceased all medical therapy and died of visceral leishmaniasis complications within one month.
